PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Poems, songs and passages can carry lessons about a clean environment. In this sub-strand you will read them with expression, stress and rhythm, answer questions, and explain proverbs such as 'Many hands make light work' and 'A stitch in time saves nine'. Intensive reading means you read until you understand, not only until you finish the lines.

## Strand 12.0: Clean Environment
Sub-strand 12.2.1: Reading: Intensive Reading (Poems, Songs and Passages)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read a poem, song or passage containing proverbs with expression for effective communication
b) apply basic stress and rhythm when reading a poem, song or passage containing proverbs for self-expression
c) respond to questions based on a poem, song or passage containing proverbs for comprehension
d) adopt intensive reading in day-to-day communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Poem
• Song
• Passage
• Proverbs

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we enjoy reading poems?
2. How are poems different from stories?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner discusses and role plays with peers events in the passage or in the song.
• Self-efficacy: This is achieved as the learner answers questions from songs and poems, and takes part in the role play confidently.

## Values
• Responsibility: It is inculcated in the learner as they take upon assigned duties of reading the poems, discussing the events and identifying the proverbs in the passage.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Online Safety: The learner’s knowledge on personal safety is emphasised when accessing internet resources to watch a video on how people recite poems.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner applies the skills acquired in reading intensively to their learning of reading skills in other areas such as Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 12.0 Clean Environment, Sub-strand 12.2.1 Intensive Reading: Poems, Songs and Passages

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Reading a poem with stress and rhythm

LESSON 1: READING A POEM WITH STRESS AND RHYTHM
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Read a poem aloud with expression.
• Mark the strong beats that make the rhythm.
• Say how a poem differs from a story.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a poem, song or passage containing proverbs with expression for effective communication; b) apply basic stress and rhythm when reading a poem, song or passage containing proverbs for self-expression

## Introduction
A story walks from event to event. A poem often marches. The beats in the lines help you remember the message. Listen for the strong words as you read.

## Notes
### Stress and rhythm
Stress is the stronger push you give to an important syllable or word. Rhythm is the pattern those pushes make, like a drum. In a poem we usually stress the words that carry meaning and lighten the small words.

Read the line in two ways. First, every word the same size: bring a broom and sweep the path. Second, with stress: BRING a BROOM and SWEEP the PATH. The second reading has a beat. Your foot can tap on bring, broom, sweep and path.

Do not shout the stressed words. Make them a little louder or a little longer. Keep the rhythm steady from line to line.

### The Path We Share
Bring a broom and sweep the path,
Clear the drain beside the grass.
Many hands make light work:
Pick the paper as you pass.

Water trees along the fence,
Keep the rubbish in the pit.
A stitch in time saves nine:
Mend the leak before it splits.

Green hills, clean rivers, quiet yards,
These are ours to care for still.
Waste not, want not, every day,
Leave the compound cleaner still.

### Two proverbs in the poem
'Many hands make light work' means a job is easier when people share it. Ten learners can clear a path faster than one.

'A stitch in time saves nine' means a small repair done early saves a much bigger repair later. Closing a small leak today can stop a wasted pool of water tomorrow.

'Waste not, want not' means that if we do not waste things, we are less likely to lack them later.

### Poem or story?
A story is usually written in sentences and paragraphs and tells events in order. A poem is written in lines and stanzas. It often has rhythm, and it may repeat a pattern. Both can teach. We enjoy poems because the beat, the pictures and the short lines make a message stick in the memory.

When you read this poem, smile on the working lines, slow down on 'Mend the leak', and keep the beats even. Expression and rhythm together make the meaning clear.

## Key words
• stress — the stronger beat we give to an important word or syllable
• rhythm — the pattern of strong and weak beats in a line
• stanza — a group of lines in a poem
• proverb — a short, well-known saying that teaches a lesson

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which words would you stress in 'Pick the paper as you pass'?

Working:
1. Choose the words that carry the picture.
2. Leave the small words lighter.

Answer: Pick, paper and pass.

### Example 2
What does 'A stitch in time saves nine' mean in the poem?

Working:
1. Look at the line that follows the proverb.
2. It tells you to mend a leak early.

Answer: Repair a small problem early so that it does not become a big one. In the poem, mend the leak before it splits.

## Activity: Tap the beat
You will need: A copy of the poem, A desk to tap lightly
1. Listen once while a leader reads the poem and taps the strong beats.
2. In pairs, mark four stressed words in the first stanza and read the stanza together.
3. Read the whole poem with expression: steady speed, clear proverbs, a slower voice on the warning about the leak.
4. Tell your partner one way this poem is different from a story.

## Practice
1. What is stress in reading?
2. What does 'Many hands make light work' mean?
3. Name two ways a poem can differ from a story.
4. Why should the line about mending the leak be read carefully?

## Summary
• Stress the meaningful words to make a rhythm.
• The poem uses proverbs to teach care for the compound.
• Poems use lines and beats; stories use paragraphs and events.

### Answers to practice
1. The stronger beat given to an important word or syllable.
2. A job is easier when people do it together.
3. A poem is written in lines and often has rhythm. A story is written in paragraphs and tells events in order.
4. It carries a warning: a small leak should be mended before it becomes a bigger problem.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: A passage with proverbs

LESSON 2: A PASSAGE WITH PROVERBS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Read a passage and find the proverbs.
• Answer factual and inferential questions.
• Explain what each proverb means in the passage.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a poem, song or passage containing proverbs with expression for effective communication; c) respond to questions based on a poem, song or passage containing proverbs for comprehension

## Introduction
A proverb is short, but a passage can show it at work. As you read, watch for the sayings and for the events that explain them.

## Notes
### Saturday on the Compound
Last Saturday our class cleaned the neighbourhood around the school. The grass was long, the drain was blocked, and paper had blown under a bush. Our teacher looked at the mess and said, 'Many hands make light work.' She was right. Learners with brooms finished the path much faster than one person could have done alone.

Near a tree we found a cracked pipe. Only a thin line of water was escaping, but the ground around it was already soft. I remembered the saying 'A stitch in time saves nine.' We did not walk past the leak. We told the school keeper. He closed the tap so that more water would not be wasted while the pipe waited to be mended. Stopping a small leak early was wiser than waiting for mud and a larger repair.

Before we went home we sorted the rubbish. Fruit peels went into a pit, where they could rot and help the soil. Plastic went into a sack to be taken away. The keeper nodded and said, 'Waste not, want not.' If we throw away things that can still be used, we may need them later and find them gone.

By afternoon the drain was clear, the bin was in its place and the compound looked calm. Someone said, 'Cleanliness is next to godliness.' I take that proverb to mean that keeping a place clean is a worthy habit, because it shows care for other people. I understood the words when I saw the open drain running and the grass free of paper.

### Reading for meaning
A factual question asks for a detail that is written down: What was wrong with the drain? An inferential question asks you to think: Why did the keeper close the tap? The passage does not say the words 'to stop waste' in that sentence, but the leak and the proverb point you there.

Read the proverbs again and give each one a meaning in your own words. A proverb you can explain is a proverb you can use.

## Key words
• factual question — a question answered by a detail stated in the text
• inferential question — a question you answer by thinking about clues in the text
• keeper — a person who looks after a place such as a school
• neighbourhood — the area around your home or school

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Factual: What did the class do with fruit peels and with plastic?

Working:
1. Find the paragraph about sorting rubbish.
2. Each material went to a different place.

Answer: Fruit peels went into a pit. Plastic went into a sack.

### Example 2
Inferential: Why was closing the tap a good example of 'A stitch in time saves nine'?

Working:
1. The leak was still small.
2. Acting early prevented a bigger waste and a bigger mess.

Answer: The leak was small. Closing the tap early stopped more water from being wasted and kept the problem from growing.

## Activity: Proverbs in action
You will need: The passage, Exercise books
1. Read the passage silently, then aloud in groups, one paragraph each.
2. Underline the four proverbs.
3. Write the meaning of each proverb in your own words.
4. Role play the moment when the class finds the leak and tells the keeper. Use one proverb in the scene.

## Practice
1. Which proverb did the teacher use at the start, and why did it fit?
2. What was wrong with the pipe?
3. What does 'Waste not, want not' mean in this passage?
4. Why does the writer agree that cleanliness shows care?

## Summary
• The passage shows four proverbs through a class clean-up.
• Factual questions use stated details. Inferential questions use clues.
• Explain a proverb in your own words to show that you understand it.

### Answers to practice
1. Many hands make light work. It fitted because the class shared the cleaning and finished faster.
2. It was cracked, and a thin line of water was escaping.
3. If we do not throw away things that can still be used, we will not lack them later.
4. A clear drain and grass free of paper make the place safer and pleasanter for other people.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: A song, a role play and a reading habit

LESSON 3: A SONG, A ROLE PLAY AND A READING HABIT
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Sing or read a short song with rhythm.
• Answer questions about the song and the passage.
• Explain how intensive reading helps everyday life.

Curriculum outcomes: c) respond to questions based on a poem, song or passage containing proverbs for comprehension; d) adopt intensive reading in day-to-day communication

## Introduction
A song is a poem with a tune. Even if you only chant it, the rhythm has to stay steady or the words tumble. Today the words remind us what to do with a broom, a bin and a leak.

## Notes
### Clear the Compound
Sweep, sweep, sweep the path,
Bring the broom and clear the grass.
Many hands make light work,
Pick the rubbish as we pass.

Waste not, want not, use the bin,
Water trees and tuck them in.
A stitch in time saves nine,
Mend the fence and clear the drain.

Clap on sweep, broom, grass and pass in the first stanza. Clap on waste, want, bin and trees, then on stitch, nine, fence and drain. The claps are the rhythm. Your voice can grow brighter on the working lines and firmer on the two proverbs.

### Questions a careful reader can answer
Who is speaking? A group, because the song says 'we'. What should be mended or cleared? The fence and the drain. Which proverb tells us to share the job? 'Many hands make light work.' Which proverb tells us not to throw useful things away? 'Waste not, want not.'

If you only sing the tune and miss the words, you miss the lesson. Intensive reading means you slow down, reread a line, and make sure you can answer a question without guessing.

### Using the habit
You can read intensively outside this lesson. When a notice tells the class to clear the drain, read who must go, where, and when. When a poem is recited on a video, listen for the proverb and be ready to say what it means. Ask an adult before you open a video, and leave a page that is unkind or confusing.

Intensive reading helps you follow instructions, enjoy poems and songs, and explain ideas to someone else. That is a habit worth keeping every week, not only on the day you study proverbs.

## Key words
• intensive reading — reading carefully so that you understand the meaning, not only the sounds
• stanza — a grouped set of lines in a poem or song
• chant — to say or sing words in a steady rhythm

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which proverb in the song tells the singers to share the work?

Working:
1. Look for a saying, not an ordinary instruction.
2. Match it to the idea of working together.

Answer: Many hands make light work.

### Example 2
Why is it not enough to clap the rhythm and ignore the words?

Working:
1. The rhythm carries the tune.
2. The words carry the instruction and the proverb.

Answer: Because the lesson is in the words. Missing them means missing what to do and what the proverbs mean.

## Activity: Sing, act and explain
You will need: The song, A broom or a picture of one, Space to role play
1. Chant or sing the song together, clapping the strong beats.
2. Watch a short recitation if your teacher plays one, and note any proverb you hear. If there is no video, listen to a classmate recite the poem from the first lesson.
3. Role play a clean-up. One learner gives an instruction, another uses a proverb, and the group acts it out.
4. Answer the practice questions in writing, then discuss one way you will use intensive reading this week.

## Practice
1. What two things does the second stanza tell you to mend or clear?
2. Which proverb means we should not waste useful things?
3. What is intensive reading?
4. Give one everyday use of intensive reading.

## Summary
• A song needs both rhythm and understood words.
• The song repeats proverbs you can explain and act.
• Intensive reading helps you follow instructions and enjoy poems every week.

### Answers to practice
1. The fence and the drain.
2. Waste not, want not.
3. Reading carefully until you understand, so you can answer questions and explain the meaning.
4. Example: Reading a notice carefully so you know who must clear the drain, where and when.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 12.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING (POEMS, SONGS AND PASSAGES)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Stress in reading means
   A. reading with no voice
   B. giving a stronger beat to important words
   C. skipping every second line
   D. writing in capital letters only

2. Which words carry the beat in 'BRING a BROOM and SWEEP the PATH'?
   A. a, and, the
   B. bring, broom, sweep, path
   C. only the word and
   D. none of them

3. 'Many hands make light work' means
   A. one person should do everything
   B. a shared job is easier
   C. hands should stay in pockets
   D. work must be done in the dark

4. In the poem, 'A stitch in time saves nine' is followed by the idea of
   A. ignoring a leak
   B. mending a leak early
   C. cutting down every tree
   D. throwing paper on the grass

5. In the passage, fruit peels were put
   A. in a sack with the plastic
   B. into a pit
   C. into the drain
   D. on the grass

6. Why did the keeper close the tap?
   A. to water the paper
   B. so more water would not be wasted from the cracked pipe
   C. to fill the classroom
   D. to hide the brooms

7. 'Waste not, want not' in the passage means
   A. throw everything away
   B. if we do not waste useful things, we are less likely to lack them later
   C. never use a bin
   D. buy new brooms every day

8. Which proverb in the song tells singers to share the job?
   A. Waste not, want not
   B. Many hands make light work
   C. A stitch in time saves nine
   D. Cleanliness is next to godliness

9. What is intensive reading?

10. Why is intensive reading useful beyond the lesson?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 12.2.1 READING: INTENSIVE READING (POEMS, SONGS AND PASSAGES)
========================================

1. B. giving a stronger beat to important words
   Stress is the stronger beat on important words or syllables.

2. B. bring, broom, sweep, path
   Those four words are the strong beats.

3. B. a shared job is easier
   The proverb means people finish a job more easily together.

4. B. mending a leak early
   The next line says to mend the leak before it splits.

5. B. into a pit
   Fruit peels went into a pit to help the soil.

6. B. so more water would not be wasted from the cracked pipe
   He stopped the leak from wasting more water while the pipe waited to be mended.

7. B. if we do not waste useful things, we are less likely to lack them later
   The keeper's saying warns against throwing away what can still be used.

8. B. Many hands make light work
   That line is in the first stanza of the song.

9. Reading carefully until you understand the meaning and can answer questions about it.
   It is understanding, not only saying the words.

10. It helps you follow notices and instructions, enjoy poems and songs, and explain ideas to other people.
   The habit serves everyday communication.

=================================================

Clap on sweep, broom, grass and pass in the first stanza. Clap on waste, want, bin and trees, then on stitch, nine, fence and drain. The claps are the rhythm. Your voice can grow brighter on the working lines and firmer on the two proverbs.

### Questions a careful reader can answer
Who is speaking? A group, because the song says 'we'. What should be mended or cleared? The fence and the drain. Which proverb tells us to share the job? 'Many hands make light work.' Which proverb tells us not to throw useful things away? 'Waste not, want not.'

If you only sing the tune and miss the words, you miss the lesson. Intensive reading means you slow down, reread a line, and make sure you can answer a question without guessing.

### Using the habit
You can read intensively outside this lesson. When a notice tells the class to clear the drain, read who must go, where, and when. When a poem is recited on a video, listen for the proverb and be ready to say what it means. Ask an adult before you open a video, and leave a page that is unkind or confusing.

Intensive reading helps you follow instructions, enjoy poems and songs, and explain ideas to someone else. That is a habit worth keeping every week, not only on the day you study proverbs.

## Key words
• intensive reading — reading carefully so that you understand the meaning, not only the sounds
• stanza — a grouped set of lines in a poem or song
• chant — to say or sing words in a steady rhythm

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which proverb in the song tells the singers to share the work?

Working:
1. Look for a saying, not an ordinary instruction.
2. Match it to the idea of working together.

Answer: Many hands make light work.

### Example 2
Why is it not enough to clap the rhythm and ignore the words?

Working:
1. The rhythm carries the tune.
2. The words carry the instruction and the proverb.

Answer: Because the lesson is in the words. Missing them means missing what to do and what the proverbs mean.

## Activity: Sing, act and explain
You will need: The song, A broom or a picture of one, Space to role play
1. Chant or sing the song together, clapping the strong beats.
2. Watch a short recitation if your teacher plays one, and note any proverb you hear. If there is no video, listen to a classmate recite the poem from the first lesson.
3. Role play a clean-up. One learner gives an instruction, another uses a proverb, and the group acts it out.
4. Answer the practice questions in writing, then discuss one way you will use intensive reading this week.

## Practice
1. What two things does the second stanza tell you to mend or clear?
2. Which proverb means we should not waste useful things?
3. What is intensive reading?
4. Give one everyday use of intensive reading.

## Summary
• A song needs both rhythm and understood words.
• The song repeats proverbs you can explain and act.
• Intensive reading helps you follow instructions and enjoy poems every week.

### Answers to practice
1. The fence and the drain.
2. Waste not, want not.
3. Reading carefully until you understand, so you can answer questions and explain the meaning.
4. Example: Reading a notice carefully so you know who must clear the drain, where and when.

questions.question: Stress in reading means
options: giving a stronger beat to important words
questions.explanation: Stress is the stronger beat on important words or syllables.

questions.question: Which words carry the beat in 'BRING a BROOM and SWEEP the PATH'?
questions.explanation: Those four words are the strong beats.

questions.question: 'Many hands make light work' means
options: work must be done in the dark
questions.explanation: The proverb means people finish a job more easily together.

questions.question: In the poem, 'A stitch in time saves nine' is followed by the idea of
questions.explanation: The next line says to mend the leak before it splits.

questions.question: In the passage, fruit peels were put
options: in a sack with the plastic
questions.explanation: Fruit peels went into a pit to help the soil.

questions.question: Why did the keeper close the tap?
options: so more water would not be wasted from the cracked pipe
questions.explanation: He stopped the leak from wasting more water while the pipe waited to be mended.

questions.question: 'Waste not, want not' in the passage means
options: if we do not waste useful things, we are less likely to lack them later
questions.explanation: The keeper's saying warns against throwing away what can still be used.

questions.question: Which proverb in the song tells singers to share the job?
options: A stitch in time saves nine
questions.explanation: That line is in the first stanza of the song.

questions.question: What is intensive reading?
questions.answer: Reading carefully until you understand the meaning and can answer questions about it.
questions.explanation: It is understanding, not only saying the words.

questions.question: Why is intensive reading useful beyond the lesson?
questions.answer: It helps you follow notices and instructions, enjoy poems and songs, and explain ideas to other people.
